title: He Won Gold on Tuesday. He Was Shot Dead on Friday. Para-Athlete Chirag Tyagi Was Twenty-Five.
excerpt: Tyagi had just qualified for the Para Asian Games in Japan. His alleged killer is a fellow athlete whose eligibility he had challenged.
body:
Chirag Tyagi ran the 400 metres in 50.12 seconds at the Indian Open Para Athletics International Championship in Bengaluru last week. It was fast enough for gold in the T12 category. It was fast enough to qualify him for the Para Asian Games in Nagoya this October. He called his uncle at 8:10 on Friday morning to say he was coming home to Ghaziabad from his hostel at the Sports Authority of India complex in Delhi.

His body was found at 12:30 that night in the Sai Upvan forest area, fifty metres from GT Road. A passerby heard a phone ringing in the dark.

A Farmer's Son Who Ran

Tyagi, twenty-five, was from Basantpur Sathli village in Muradnagar, Ghaziabad. His father is a farmer. He competed in running events for the visually impaired across multiple categories — T12 for the 400m, T36 for the 100m. Two days before his death, he had won both a gold in the 400 metres and a silver in the 100 metres at the National Para Athletics Championship. At the Dubai 2026 Para Athletics Grand Prix earlier this year, he took bronze in the men's 100m T36 event.

He had represented Uttar Pradesh at national competitions for years. His qualification for the Para Asian Games — India's most significant para-athletics delegation to Japan — was the culmination of a career built from a village in western UP.

The Accusation That Preceded It

Police identified the suspect within hours. CCTV footage from the area led them to Yash Khatik, a fellow para-athlete who had trained alongside Tyagi. Both competed in categories for visually impaired athletes.

According to investigators, Tyagi had filed a complaint against Khatik concerning the verification of his disability documents. That complaint led to Khatik's disqualification from competition and, critically, the nullification of his own Asian Para Games qualification.

"Prima facie, the case appears to be a murder," said Dhawal Jaiswal, DCP Ghaziabad. "CCTV footage showed a suspect who was detained and questioned. He confessed to the murder. The accused has been identified as Yash Khatik."

Khatik has been arrested. Police are working to recover the weapon.

What It Exposes

Para-athletics in India operates in a system where classification fraud — athletes competing under false disability categories — has been a persistent problem. The verification process that Tyagi triggered against Khatik is exactly the kind of integrity check the system is supposed to rely on. That it allegedly led to his murder exposes the desperation that surrounds selection for international competitions, where government jobs, stipends, and recognition are all tied to medals and qualifications.

For the Indian diaspora, the story carries a familiar weight. Para-sports funding in India has improved significantly since the 2016 Rio Paralympics, but the infrastructure around athlete safety, dispute resolution, and classification integrity remains fragile. Tyagi's death is not a failure of athletics — it is a failure of the system that surrounds it.

A Career Cut Short

Tyagi's uncle, Rajesh Tyagi, told reporters that Chirag always called ahead when he was coming home from Delhi. "He first called his father, but when the call was not answered, he informed my younger brother," Rajesh said. "After Chirag's call, we received a call from the police informing us that his body had been found."

The Para Asian Games are scheduled for October 2026 in Nagoya, Japan. Chirag Tyagi will not be there. He will not run the 400 metres in the stadium he had earned the right to enter. His gold medal from Bengaluru, won days earlier, is now the last race of his life.

He was twenty-five years old.

Sources: The Bridge, NDTV, Devdiscourse, Dainik Bhaskar
author: Diaspora Desk
